diagnostic_evidence.quote: For all $p \in \mathbb{N}$ with~$p \geq 1$, $h > 0$, and $\mu \in \R$, the variational formulation~\eqref{eq:10} admits a unique solution.

Let Assumption \ref{assu:34} be satisfied. Then, for all~$p \in \N$ and~$\rho \in \R$, the family of matrices~$\{\K_n^p(\rho)\}_n$ defined in~\eqref{eq:21} is weakly well-conditioned. In other words, the variational formulation in \eqref{eq:10} is unconditionally stable.

issues.failure_explanation: The abstract states unconditional stability without qualification, but the supporting Theorem 3.13 is conditional on Assumption 3.4, which is explicitly an unproven fundamental assumption for p>1. Thus the paper does not establish unconditional stability independently of this assumption.

failure_location.quote: We investigate the stability and conservation properties of the method, demonstrating that it preserves both mass and energy at the final time, and it is unconditionally stable.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add the qualification 'under Assumption 3.4' to the abstract and introduction, or prove Assumption 3.4.
issues.overall_effect: The main advertised guarantee is overstated; the method is proven unconditionally stable only under an additional uniqueness assumption.
issues.title: Abstract claims unconditional stability without Assumption 3.4
issues.why_classification: The formal theorem is correctly qualified; the repair is a local qualification of prose and does not alter the mathematical development.

issues.failure_explanation: The term (∂t ψ, w) in (14) is real, so its product with i is purely imaginary and has zero real part. The displayed equation incorrectly puts this real integral into the real part and also mixes it with the real part of (ψ,w) from (15). The correct argument must separate real and imaginary parts; as written, the inference to ψ≡0 is invalid.

failure_location.quote: Inserting \eqref{eq:14} and \eqref{eq:15} in \eqref{eq:13}, we conclude  \begin{equation*} 0 = \text{Re}(\mi (\dpt \psi, w)_{J_T} + \mu (\psi,w)_{J_T}) = \int_0^T |\partial_s \psi(s)|^2 e^{-s/T} \dd s +  \frac{\mu}{2T} \int_0^T |\psi(s)|^2 e^{-s/T} \dd s + \frac{\mu}{2e} |\psi(T)|^2, \end{equation*}

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the final inference by the correct split: taking the real part gives μ Re(ψ,w)=0; if μ≠0, (15) forces ψ≡0; if μ=0, taking the imaginary part and (14) forces ∂tψ=0, hence ψ≡0.
issues.overall_effect: The proof of uniqueness in Proposition 3.2 is unsupported as written.
issues.title: Invalid real-part inference in uniqueness proof of Proposition 3.2
issues.why_classification: The result is true and the repair is a short local correction of the real/imaginary part argument.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: q^{\mathbf{B}^p}(e^{\mi \theta}) = - e^{\mi p \theta}  B_p(\theta), \quad\quad q^{\mathbf{C}^p}(e^{\mi \theta}) = - e^{\mi p \theta}\mi C_p(\theta).
q^{\mathbf{K}^p(\rho)}(e^{\mi \theta})  =  \mi e^{\mi p \theta}( - B_p(\theta) + \rho C_p(\theta)), \quad \rho \in \R, \ \theta \in [-\pi,\pi], \text{~and~} p \in \N.

issues.failure_explanation: Using the displayed expression, q^K(e^{iθ}) = i e^{ipθ}(-B_p(θ)+ρ C_p(θ)). Since B_p is even and C_p is odd, q^K(e^{-iθ}) = i e^{-ipθ}(-B_p(θ)-ρ C_p(θ)), which is not a constant multiple of q^K(e^{iθ}) unless ρ C_p=0. For p=1, B_1(θ)=2cosθ-2 and C_1(θ)=-sinθ give q^K(z)=(ρ/2-i)+2iz+(-i-ρ/2)z^2, whose coefficients a_0 and a_2 are unequal for ρ≠0. Thus q^K is not reciprocal for general ρ.

failure_location.quote: The symbol polynomial $q^{\mathbf{K}^p(\rho)}$ of the family $\{ \K_n^p(\rho) \}_n$ defined in \eqref{eq:21} is a reciprocal polynomial.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the false reciprocity claim with a direct zero-counting argument for q^K, e.g., using q^K(e^{iθ}) = i e^{ipθ}K_p(θ) and the sign changes of K_p, to show it has type (p-1,2,p-1) for ρ≠0 (and handle ρ=0 separately).
issues.overall_effect: The proof of weak well-conditioning of K_n^p(ρ) via the reciprocal-polynomial argument fails. This undermines the proof of Theorem 3.13 and, in turn, the stability proof of Theorem 4.2.
issues.title: Proposition 3.9 falsely claims the symbol polynomial q^K is reciprocal
issues.why_classification: The false proposition invalidates a central step, but the main stability result can likely be recovered by a contained nontrivial zero-counting argument rather than a wholly new architecture.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: For~$\rho>0$ and~$p \in \mathbb{N}$, the function $K_p(\theta,\rho)$ has exactly 2 simple zeros $\theta \in [-\pi,\pi]$.

\lim_{\theta \to 0} B_p(\theta) = \lim_{\theta \to 0}  C_p(\theta) = 0 , \quad  C_p(-\pi)=C_p(\pi)=0, \quad B_p(\pi)=B_p(-\pi)<0, \\  \lim_{\theta \to 0} B_p'(\theta) = 0, \quad \lim_{\theta \to 0} C_p'(\theta) = -1.

issues.failure_explanation: Proposition 3.12 only covers ρ>0. For ρ=0, q^K(e^{iθ}) = i e^{ipθ}(-B_p(θ)). The limits in (27) give B_p(0)=B_p'(0)=0, so θ=0 is a zero of multiplicity at least two. There are not two simple zeros as claimed for all ρ∈R. Thus the proof of Theorem 3.13 does not cover ρ=0.

failure_location.quote: The aim of this section is to derive an explicit expression for $q^{\K^p(\rho)}(e^{\mi \theta})$ with~$\theta \in [-\pi,\pi]$ and subsequently show that, for all $p \in \mathbb{N}$ and $\rho \in \R$, there exist exactly two values of $\theta$, both with multiplicity one, such that $q^{\K^p(\rho)}(e^{\mi \theta}) = 0$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Handle ρ=0 separately by counting the double zero at θ=0 as two unit zeros, or extend Proposition 3.12 to include ρ=0 with multiplicity.
issues.overall_effect: The proof of Theorem 3.13 is incomplete for ρ=0; the theorem's conclusion for this parameter is not established by the given argument.
issues.title: Step 4 misses the degenerate case ρ=0 in the zero-counting claim
issues.why_classification: The missing degenerate case is local and the conclusion remains true with a standard multiplicity adjustment.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Let Assumption \ref{assu:34} be satisfied. Then, for all~$p \in \N$ and~$\rho \in \R$, the family of matrices~$\{\K_n^p(\rho)\}_n$ defined in~\eqref{eq:21} is weakly well-conditioned.
Assume that, for all $p \in \N$ with $p \ge 1$, $h>0$, and $\mu_w > 0$ the variational formulation~\eqref{eq:30} admits a unique solution.

issues.failure_explanation: Theorem 3.13 is conditional on Assumption 3.4, which is not assumed in Theorem 4.2. The uniqueness assumption on (30) does not by itself provide Assumption 3.4 for all μ. Although it may imply the needed nonsingularity for the specific choice μ_s=-1, this is not stated or used, so the invocation of Theorem 3.13 is outside its hypotheses.

failure_location.quote: Theorem \ref{th:313} guarantees the stability of the variational formulation~\eqref{eq:10}, and, consequently, that of~\eqref{eq:32}.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Either add Assumption 3.4 to Theorem 4.2, or use a fixed-ρ version of Theorem 3.13 and show that the uniqueness assumption on (30) supplies the needed nonsingularity for μ_s=-1.
issues.overall_effect: The proof of Theorem 4.2 is invalid as written; the unconditional stability of (30) is not established by this argument.
issues.title: Theorem 4.2 invokes Theorem 3.13 without its Assumption 3.4
issues.why_classification: The needed hypothesis can likely be derived for the specific parameter, making this a local dependency gap rather than a loss of the main result.

issues.failure_explanation: Lemma A.1 gives an upper bound on the condition number of the Schur complement S in terms of the block matrix M. From M weakly well-conditioned, it implies S weakly well-conditioned. The proof then needs the converse: from S weakly well-conditioned to M_w weakly well-conditioned. Lemma A.1 does not provide this reverse implication, and no other argument is given.

failure_location.quote: Hence, the weakly well-conditioning of these Schur complements implies the stability of formulation~\eqref{eq:30}.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add a reverse bound, e.g., using the block inverse formula for M_w, showing that if B and S are weakly well-conditioned and C is bounded independently of h, then M_w is weakly well-conditioned.
issues.overall_effect: The final step of Theorem 4.2 is unsupported; the stability of (30) does not follow from the Schur complement conditioning alone via the stated lemma.
issues.title: Theorem 4.2 uses Lemma A.1 in the wrong direction
issues.why_classification: A contained nontrivial argument is needed to close the proof, but the conclusion may still survive.

issues.failure_explanation: The Schur transformation of (35) should lead to a system of the form (I⊗M + R⊗A)Z = -i(Q^H B^{-1}⊗I)F (up to ordering), not (R⊗A + R^{-1}⊗M)Z = Y. In the scalar case B=C=M=A=1, the Schur value is R=(i)^{-1}=-i, so the step-4 matrix is -i+i=0, singular, while the original matrix i+1 is invertible. Thus the algorithm fails to solve (35) in general.

issues.overall_effect: Algorithm 5.1 does not provide the claimed efficient solver for the linear system (35); the numerical implementation described is invalid as stated.
